screens.title: Out of balance
screens.text: A was just inserted, and node G now has balance factor −2. How would you fix it?
options: Sort all the keys and rebuild the tree
Lift C up and let G move down
screens.answer: Lift C up and let G move down
screens.reveal: Rebuilding from sorted keys works but needs sorting every time a key is added. A rotation fixes the balance locally, by moving a child up and its parent down, without breaking the BST order.

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: Identify and perform the single or double rotation that restores AVL balance (LO4).

task.stem: An in-order traversal of a BST lists the keys in which order?
task.hint: This checks that you can verify a result: the in-order keys must still be sorted, and every balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1.

options.explanation: Right. That is why an in-order check can show that a rotation kept the BST order.
In-order means left subtree, node, right subtree, which gives sorted order whatever the insertion order.

options.text: Level by level, from the root down

screens.title: Right rotation, step by step
screens.text: A single rotation swaps the roles of a child and its parent without breaking the BST order. Here child C = 30 rotates around parent P = 50, whose parent is G = 80.
screens.caption: Right rotation: the parent becomes the right child of its left child.
roleSteps: 1. The grandparent G (80) of child C (30) becomes C’s parent, replacing P (50).
2. The right subtree of C (40) becomes the left subtree of P (50).
3. C (30) takes P (50) as its right child.

screens.title: Left rotation
screens.text: The mirror image: child 40 rotates around parent 20.
screens.caption: Left rotation: the parent becomes the left child of its right child.
roleSteps: 1. 40 takes 20’s place at the top of this subtree.
2. The left subtree of 40 (30) becomes the right subtree of 20.

screens.title: The four cases
points: Case 1 (LL): the new key is in the left subtree of the left child of n. Fix: right rotation about n.
Case 2 (LR): right subtree of the left child. Fix: left rotation about n.left, then right rotation about n.
Case 3 (RL): left subtree of the right child. Fix: right rotation about n.right, then left rotation about n.
Case 4 (RR): right subtree of the right child. Fix: left rotation about n.
Cases 1 and 4 are on the “outside” and need one rotation. Cases 2 and 3 are on the “inside” and need two (a double rotation).
screens.showRule: Outside (LL, RR): single rotation. Inside (LR, RL): double rotation.

screens.title: Case 1: one right rotation
screens.text: Back to the opening tree. A went into the left subtree of G’s left child C: Case 1.
screens.caption: Rotate C around G: a single right rotation about the unbalanced node.
steps: A goes in the empty left branch of B.
Node G has balance factor −2: it is the first unbalanced node, n. Case 1 (LL).
Rotate C around G: right rotation about G.
Every node has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.

screens.title: Why one rotation is not always enough
screens.text: Here E went into the right subtree of G’s left child: Case 2, an inside case. Watch what a single right rotation does.
screens.caption: The single rotation only moves the problem: C now has balance factor +2.
steps: Rotate C around G: right rotation about G.

screens.title: Case 2: the double rotation
screens.text: First a left rotation about n.left (C), which turns Case 2 into Case 1. Then a right rotation about n (G).
screens.caption: Rotate D around C, then rotate D around G.
steps: Rotate D around C: left rotation about C.
Rotate D around G: right rotation about G.

task.stem: 6 was just inserted, and the tree is out of balance. Select the unbalanced node and choose the rotation that fixes it.
task.hint: This checks that you can carry out the rotation(s): the child moves up around its parent, and its inner subtree changes sides.

wrongAnswers.feedback: Rotate towards the shorter branch: if n’s left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation; if its right branch is too tall, a left rotation.
Fix the first unbalanced node on the way up from the new key (8), not the root.

feedback.correct: Node 8 is n (bf −2). 6 went into the left subtree of 8’s left child, so this is Case 1: a single right rotation about 8. The textbook shows this example in Figure 4.32.
feedback.incorrect: Node 8 is n (bf −2). 6 went into the left subtree of 8’s left child, so this is Case 1: a single right rotation about 8. The textbook shows this example in Figure 4.32.

task.stem: 15 was just inserted. Find n and perform the rotation(s).
task.hint: This checks that you can carry out the rotation(s): the child moves up around its parent, and its inner subtree changes sides.

wrongAnswers.feedback: For an inside case, rotate about n’s child first (this turns it into an outside case), then about n.
Rotate towards the shorter branch: if n’s left branch is too tall, the final rotation about n is a right rotation; if its right branch is too tall, a left rotation.
Fix the first unbalanced node on the way up from the new key (7), not the root.

feedback.correct: Node 7 is n (bf +2). 15 went into the left subtree of 7’s right child (16): Case 3. Right rotation about 16, then left rotation about 7. This is the textbook’s running example.
feedback.incorrect: Node 7 is n (bf +2). 15 went into the left subtree of 7’s right child (16): Case 3. Right rotation about 16, then left rotation about 7. This is the textbook’s running example.

task.stem: Here is the tree after your rotations. How can you check that it is correct?
task.hint: This checks that you can verify a result: the in-order keys must still be sorted, and every balance factor must be −1, 0 or +1.

options.text: Check that the in-order keys are still sorted and that every balance factor is −1, 0 or +1
options.explanation: Right. A rotation must keep the BST order and restore the AVL rule.

options.text: Check only that the in-order keys are still sorted
options.explanation: A sorted in-order shows the BST order is kept, but not that the tree is balanced.

options.text: Check only the balance factor of the root
options.explanation: Every node must have bf −1, 0 or +1, not just the root.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: One question for each assessment criterion of this lesson’s objective. Each question allows one re-attempt, and the hint is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: A rotation moves a child up around its parent and keeps the in-order sequence.
Outside cases (1 and 4): one rotation. Inside cases (2 and 3): two rotations.
Always check the result: in-order still sorted, every bf −1, 0 or +1.
